function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑reference cheat sheet for pulling “detailed” interface data on the most common platforms. If you’re working against a particular vendor’s API (e.g., a Cisco/Juniper/Arista RESTCONF/NETCONF endpoint), let me know and I’ll tailor the example to that stack. --- ## 1️⃣ Linux / Unix | Tool | What it shows | Typical command | |------|---------------|-----------------| | **`ip`** | Full IP configuration, MAC, MTU, state, flags, traffic stats | `ip addr show eth0` | | **`ifconfig`** | Legacy but still useful for quick lookups | `ifconfig eth0` | | **`ethtool`** | Driver, firmware, link speed, duplex, autoneg, statistics, settings | `ethtool -i eth0` – driver & firmware
`ethtool -S eth0` – raw counters | | **`ethtool -G`** | Queue stats (TX/RX) | `ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096` | | **`ethtool -N`** | Flow‑control settings | `ethtool -N eth0 rx-flow-hash udp-port` | | **`nmcli`** | NetworkManager state, IP config, DNS, routes | `nmcli device show eth0` | | **`lshw -class network`** | Hardware description (driver, bus info, capabilities) | `sudo lshw -class network -short` | | **`lspci -v`** | PCI bus details (for NICs on PCI) | `lspci -v -s $(lspci | grep Ethernet | awk '{print $1}')` | ### Example: Pull all details for `eth0` ```bash # Basic IP + MAC ip addr show eth0 # Driver & firmware ethtool -i eth0 # Raw statistics ethtool -S eth0 # Traffic queue stats ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096 # Flow‑control ethtool -N eth0 rx-flow-hash udp-port # NetworkManager view nmcli device show eth0 ``` --- ## 2️⃣ Windows | Cmdlet / Tool | What it shows | Typical command | |---------------|---------------|-----------------| | **PowerShell `Get-NetAdapter`** | Adapter name, status, MAC, speed, driver, firmware | `Get-NetAdapter -Name "Ethernet" | Format-List *` | | **PowerShell `Get-NetIPConfiguration`** | IP config, DNS, routes | `Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet"` | | **`netsh interface ipv4 show addresses`** | IPv4 addresses, gateway | `netsh interface ipv4 show addresses "Ethernet"` | | **`netsh interface ipv6 show addresses`** | IPv6 addresses | `netsh interface ipv6 show addresses "Ethernet"` | | **`wmic nic`** | Driver version, MAC, speed | `wmic nic where NetEnabled=true get Name,MACAddress,Speed,DriverVersion` | | **Device Manager** | Driver details, status | Right‑click → Properties → Driver tab | ### Example: Get everything for “Ethernet” ```powershell # Adapter properties Get-NetAdapter -Name "Ethernet" | Format-List * # IP configuration Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet" # Driver via WMI wmic nic where NetEnabled=true get Name,MACAddress,Speed,DriverVersion ``` --- ## 3️⃣ SNMP (generic) | OID | What it returns | Typical command | |-----|-----------------|-----------------| | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1` | Interface index | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifIndex` | | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2` | Interface description | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifDescr` | | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5` | Interface speed (bits/sec) | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifSpeed` | | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8` | Interface operational status | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifOperStatus` | | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` | In octets | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifInOctets` | | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16` | Out octets | `snmpwalk -v2c -c public localhost IF-MIB::ifOutOctets` | > **Tip:** Use `snmpbulkwalk` for bulk retrieval of all interfaces at once. --- ## 4️⃣ RESTCONF / NETCONF (Cisco, Juniper, Arista, etc.) | Endpoint | What it returns | Typical curl | |----------|-----------------|--------------| | `/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/gigabitethernet=1/1` | Full interface config & status | `curl -k -u admin:admin https://router/api/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface/gigabitethernet=1/1` | | `/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper:interfaces-state/interface=GigabitEthernet1/1` | Operational state | `curl -k -u admin:admin https://router/api/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper:interfaces-state/interface=GigabitEthernet1/1` | | `/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper:interfaces-state` | All interfaces | `curl -k -u admin:admin https://router/api/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper:interfaces-state` | > **Note:** Replace the base URL, credentials, and interface name per your environment. --- ## 5️⃣ Using the Provided `requests_get` Function If you have a JSON endpoint that exposes interface details (e.g., a custom monitoring service), you can fetch it like this: ```python from functions import requests_get response = requests_get({ "url": "https://monitor.example.com/api/interfaces", "params": {"detail": "full"} # optional query params }) print(response.json()) ``` Replace `"https://monitor.example.com/api/interfaces"` with the actual URL that returns the interface data in JSON format. --- ## Quick Checklist 1. **Identify the platform** (Linux, Windows, SNMP, RESTCONF, etc.). 2. **Choose the right tool**: - Linux: `ip`, `ethtool`, `nmcli`. - Windows: PowerShell cmdlets (`Get-NetAdapter`, `Get-NetIPConfiguration`). - SNMP: `snmpwalk`/`snmpbulkwalk`. - RESTCONF/NETCONF: `curl` or vendor SDK. 3. **Run the command** and capture the output. 4. **Parse the output** (e.g., `jq` for JSON, `awk`/`sed` for text). Let me know if you need a script that pulls all of this into a single JSON blob or if you’re targeting a specific vendor’s API!
